destination.title: They Took His Life Savings at the Airport — No Charges, No Crime

short34: You can fly with your life savings in cash
it's completely legal.
But at the airport
the government can take it
and never charge you with a crime.
That's what happened to Terry Rolin.
He had saved about eighty-two thousand dollars
in cash over a lifetime.
When his daughter flew with it to
put it in the bank
agents at the airport stopped her and
seized every dollar
on suspicion alone.
But on a domestic flight there is
no limit on the cash you can carry
and no form to file.
No one was charged with anything.
Under civil forfeiture
the money itself is treated as guilty
and you have to go to court
to prove your own cash is innocent.
The Institute for Justice sued on behalf
of travelers like them.
In 2022 the case ended in a settlement
and by 2025 the D-E-A had shut
down its program of seizing cash at airports.
The government gave Terry his savings back
but most people never get that far.
Watch the full story on the channel.
Follow for more.

The standard is only a "preponderance of the evidence" — more likely than not.
That is the bar your own savings would be judged by, and it sits far below the "beyond a reasonable doubt" a prosecutor needs to put someone in prison.
Federal agents took every bill, and never charged anyone with a crime.
It is late August, 2019, at Pittsburgh International Airport.
In the year 2000, Congress changed that with the Civil Asset Forfeiture Reform Act — CAFRA.
Most people never fight at all: the cash they lost is worth less than the lawyer it would take to get it back, so they let it go.
Under a federal program called equitable sharing, rooted in a 1984 crime law, the agency that seizes the cash can keep or share the proceeds.
And it runs at a scale most people never imagine: not a few hundred cases, but tens of thousands.

In 2016, a USA Today investigation, later cited in the coverage of Terry's own case, reported that between 2006 and 2015 the DEA seized more than two hundred and nine million dollars from over five thousand travelers, across fifteen major American airports.
In 2017, the Justice Department's own Office of Inspector General looked at the DEA's cash seizures.
Over roughly a decade, it reported, the agency had seized more than three point two billion dollars in cash, across about sixty-five thousand seizures, none of it connected to a criminal charge.
That is what a forfeiture looks like from the inside — an old man waiting, in pain, over money the government held and never charged him about.
By the Institute for Justice's own accounting, states and the federal government together have taken at least sixty-eight point eight billion dollars through forfeiture since the year 2000.

In an ordinary criminal case, the government charges a person.

source_lines: Because the case is against the money and not against you, the government does not have to charge you, or convict you, or even say out loud that you did anything wrong.

lines.text: In 2000 Congress made the government carry the burden. But read the fine print. The standard is only a preponderance of the evidence.

On paper it flipped the scale, so now the government has to prove the property is forfeitable.

source_lines: In plain terms, the government does not have to be sure your money is dirty. It only has to convince a judge that it is more likely dirty than not.
